text: Some time later, during the wheat harvest, Samson went to visit his wife, bringing a young goat. He said, "I'm going in to my wife, into her room." But her father would not let him in.
"I was sure you hated her," her father said, "so I gave her to your best man. Isn't her younger sister better than she is? Take her instead."
But Samson said to them, "This time I have a right to get even with the Philistines. I am going to do them real harm."
So Samson went out and caught three hundred foxes. He took torches, tied the foxes tail to tail, and fastened a torch between each pair of tails.
Then he lit the torches and turned the foxes loose in the standing grain of the Philistines. He burned the stacked sheaves and the standing grain, and the vineyards and olive groves as well.

versions.text: Then he lit the torches and turned the foxes loose in the standing grain of the Philistines. He burned up the shocks and the standing grain, along with the vineyards and olive groves.
versions.explanation: "Shocks" is archaic and unclear when read aloud; "stacked sheaves" renders גָּדִישׁ clearly. Also "along with" is smoothed to a cleaner rhythm for oral reading.

text: The Philistines asked, "Who did this?" And they were told, "Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite, because his wife was taken from him and given to his best man." So the Philistines went up and burned her and her father to death.
Samson said to them, "Since you have acted like this, I swear I will not stop until I have taken my revenge on you."
He struck them down, hip and thigh, with great slaughter. Then he went down and stayed in the cleft of the rock of Etam.

versions.text: He struck them down with great slaughter, hip and thigh. Then he went down and stayed in a cave in the rock of Etam.
versions.explanation: סְעִיף means a cleft, crevice, or crag, not a cave (מְעָרָה). "Cleft of the rock" is both more accurate and reads naturally.

versions.text: He struck them down with great slaughter, hip and thigh. Then he went down and stayed in the cleft of the rock of Etam.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew places the idiom שׁוֹק עַל־יָרֵךְ ("leg upon thigh") immediately after the verb, with מַכָּה גְדוֹלָה ("a great blow/slaughter") as the closing summary. Restoring that order gives a smoother spoken cadence and avoids the trailing, tacked-on feel of "...great slaughter, hip and thigh." A brief footnote noting that "hip and thigh" renders an obscure Hebrew idiom for a thorough, brutal defeat would also help the listener.

text: The Philistines came up and camped in Judah, spreading out near Lehi.
The men of Judah asked, "Why have you come up against us?" They answered, "We have come to take Samson prisoner, to do to him as he did to us."

Then three thousand men of Judah went down to the cleft of the rock of Etam and said to Samson, "Don't you know that the Philistines rule over us? What is this you have done to us?" He answered, "I did to them what they did to me."

versions.text: Then three thousand men of Judah went down to the cave in the rock of Etam and said to Samson, "Don't you know that the Philistines rule over us? What have you done to us?" He answered, "I did to them what they did to me."
versions.explanation: Consistency with verse 8: סְעִיף is a cleft or crag, not a cave. Also מַה־זֹּאת עָשִׂיתָ לָּנוּ carries the force of "What is this you have done to us?"

text: They said, "We have come down to tie you up and hand you over to the Philistines." Samson said, "Swear to me that you yourselves will not kill me."
"We will not," they said. "We will only tie you up and hand you over to them. We will certainly not kill you." So they bound him with two new ropes and led him up from the rock.

As he came to Lehi, the Philistines came shouting to meet him. Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him. The ropes on his arms became like flax that has burned in the fire, and the bonds fell away from his hands.
Finding a fresh jawbone of a donkey, he reached out, took it, and struck down a thousand men.

Then Samson said: "With the jawbone of a donkey, heaps upon heaps! With the jawbone of a donkey I have struck down a thousand men." [Footnote: In Hebrew the word for "donkey" and the word for "heap" sound alike, making a play on words.]

versions.text: Then Samson said: "With the jawbone of a donkey, heaps upon heaps! With the jawbone of a donkey I have struck down a thousand men."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew wordplay between חֲמוֹר (donkey) and חֲמֹרָתָיִם (heaps) is lost in English; a brief footnote helps hearers understand why the taunt is memorable.

text: When he had finished speaking, he threw the jawbone from his hand, and the place was called Ramath Lehi.
He was very thirsty, so he called out to the LORD: "You have given your servant this great victory. Must I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?"

Then God split open the hollow place at Lehi, and water came out of it. Samson drank, his strength returned, and he revived. That is why the spring is called En Hakkore, and it is at Lehi to this day.
Samson judged Israel for twenty years in the days of the Philistines.
